column2: Hearing the Brahmin's words, the Rakshasi taking forms at will, though old, became lovely-limbed, adorned with divine ornaments and jewels.
Taking the Brahmin everywhere, saying "This is my son, a mine of virtues," she goes, speaks and acts everywhere.
They took that Brahmin, adorned with beauty, fortune, youth and learning, and that old woman, endowed with virtues, to be his mother.
There a certain excellent Brahmin, putting that Rakshasi in front, gave his adorned daughter to that Brahmin.
That maiden, getting him as husband, thought, "I am fulfilled"; the Brahmin, seeing his wife endowed with virtues, was greatly distressed:

This evil-natured Rakshasi will surely eat me. What shall I do, where shall I go, to whom shall I tell this?
brahmapuran:167:21	I have fallen into great peril; who here will protect me? This wife of mine is auspicious, endowed with virtue, beauty and youth; the Rakshasi will suddenly eat her too, inauspiciously.
In the meantime his wife, full of virtue, and the old woman too, hard to approach, then went somewhere.
Bowing with modesty, young and devoted to her husband, knowing her husband distressed, she said slowly to him in private:
Why has distress come to you, master? Tell me the truth.
He slowly told his wife all as it was, in full detail from before: "What cannot be told, dear, to a friend and a woman of good family?"
Hearing her husband's words, the best of speakers said:

For one without self-control there is fear everywhere, even in houses; where is fear for those with self-control, much less on the Gautami's bank?
brahmapuran:167:28	Among those living there, devoted to Vishnu, dispassionate and discerning — bathe here, become pure, and praise the god who is free from all ills.
Hearing this, the Brahmin bathed in the Ganga, free of sin, and praised Narayana on the Gautami's bank:
You are the inner Self of this world, lord; you alone are its maker, Mukunda, and its destroyer; you are its protector, you protect; why not the wretched, protector of the unprotected, Narasimha?
Hearing his prayer, Narayana, remover of the world's grief, killed that sinful Rakshasi.
With the shining thousand-spoked Sudarshana discus, the lord gave him desired boons and brought him to his teacher.
From then on that holy place is known as the Brahmin Narayana; where wishes are fulfilled by bathing, giving, worship and the like.
There the officiating priests were sixteen, led by Vasishtha and Atri; but when the sacrificer is a Kshatriya, how can there be a ground for sacrifice?
When a Brahmin is initiated the king gives land fit for sacrifice; but when the king is initiated, who would give, and who would ask?
This begging is the mother of all misery and sinful in form; therefore no one, especially a Kshatriya, should do it.
While the Brahmins were thus debating among themselves there, the greatly wise Vasishtha, best knower of dharma, said:

When the king is being initiated, the Sun should be asked for land: 'Give me, god Savitri, a sacrificial ground fit for the gods.'
brahmapuran:168:8	'You are the divine power, Brahman, lord of beings; salutation to you.' Asked by the king, Savitri gives a pure sacrificial ground of the gods, king; so ask the lord, the Day-maker.
Saying "So be it," praised, with faith he begged the Sun, god of gods, Day-maker, of the nature of Hari and Isha:
Give, Savitri, a sacrificial ground for the gods; salutation to you. Since the Sun is the divine Kshatra, land was thus given to the king; Savitri, the lord of gods, said, "I give."
One who performs a sacrifice thus has no misfortune; likewise at a horse-sacrifice, the session with Brahmins versed in the Vedas.
Where the Sun came to the king when begun and praised, to give the gods' sacrificial ground, that is called Bhanu-tirtha.
That excellent horse-sacrifice, the gods' rite, was joined with the gods; but Daityas, Danavas and others, destroyers of sacrifice,
all wearing Brahmin disguise, singing like Sama-singers, those greatly wise ones also entered there unhindered.
They reviled the cups, vessels, soma and cup-ladles, the soma-drinking, the oblation-giving, the priests and the king;
some threw them away, other Asuras laughed. Their conduct was not known, sage, except to Vishvarupa.
Vishvarupa too said to his father, "These are Daityas." Hearing his son's word, Tvashta said to the gods:

Take water and darbha and sprinkle all around those who revile the holy sacrifice, the cup and the soma;
brahmapuran:168:19	say 'All are struck down by me' and sprinkle them.
The hosts of gods did so, and Tvashta too did likewise; then all were reduced to ashes, and became fugitives.
Saying "The great sinners are slain by me," he threw the water; then the Daityas, their lives exhausted, departed in anger.
The place where Tvashta, Prajapati of the world, cast that water is called Tvashtra-tirtha, destroyer of all sin.
Yama then killed the Daityas who had fallen from Tvashta's word, with the staff of death, the discus, the noose of death and with wrath.
Where those Daityas were slain, that holy place is called Yamya; where the sacrifice was completed, with much nectar offered in the fire,
with unbroken streams in the great sacrifice, where the oblation-bearer (Agni) was satisfied and praised —
that is called Agni-tirtha, granting the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. Indra with the Maruts said these auspicious words to the king:

You will be an emperor, king, in both worlds; and you will be my dear friend always, no doubt.
brahmapuran:168:28	Fulfilled in the human world, one should make libation at Indra-tirtha for the satisfaction of ancestors, especially at Yama-tirtha.
That holy place is Maheshvara's, where Shiva was worshipped and praised by Brahmins skilled in all rites, filled with devotion,
with Vedic and worldly mantras, with dance, songs, instruments, nectars and the five products,
with many services, prostrations and circumambulations, with incense, lamps, offerings, flowers and fragrances.
He worshipped the lord of gods, Vishnu and Shambhu, with one mind. Then the two Lords, pleased, gave boons with power;
to the praised king they gave both enjoyment and liberation, and likewise the supreme greatness of this holy place.
From then on that holy place is called Shaiva and Vaishnava; bathing and giving there, they know, grant all desires.
One who remembers or recites all these holy places is freed from all sins and goes to the city of Shiva and Vishnu.
At Bhanu-tirtha especially, bathing grants success in all aims; in that holy place of great merit there are a hundred holy places.
Hear there, great-minded one, a holy story of this kind: on the south bank of the Ganga, on the north shore of Shrigiri,
famed as Adikesha, worshipped by sages, Mahadeva always abides in linga form, granting all desires.
A sage named Sindhudvipa, exceedingly righteous; his brother named Veda was also a supreme sage.
He constantly worshipped that god Adikesha, foe of Tripura, three-eyed, with devotion, when the sun reached midday.
The clever Veda goes to the village for alms; when that excellent Brahmin has gone, a hunter, exceedingly righteous,
goes daily to hunt on that excellent holy mountain; having wandered through various countries and killed deer comfortably,
taking water in his mouth for the trident-bearer's bath, placing meat on the tip of his bow, the tired hunter, coming to the lord Shiva
at Adikesha, placing the meat outside, went to the Ganga, took water in his mouth and came to Shiva,
taking leaves of some tree in one hand with devotion and meat in the other for the offering, with his mind on him,
came to Adikesha, who had been worshipped by Veda, and with his foot struck away that worship, with the water brought in his mouth
bathed the god Shiva and worshipped him with leaves, offering that meat with the thought "May Shiva be pleased with me."
He knew nothing without auspicious devotion to Shiva; then he went to his place with the meat as he had come.
Coming and coming daily he did thus; yet the Lord was pleased with him; wonderful is the Lord's way.
As long as that Bhilla does not come, Shiva has no comfort; who knows the immeasurable compassion of Shambhu toward devotees?
Daily he worships Adikesha, Shiva with Uma; thus after a long time Veda grew angry:

Who is the sinner who destroys this wondrous worship with mantras, joined with devotion to Shiva? Let him meet death at my hands.
brahmapuran:169:18	A betrayer of teachers, gods, Brahmins and masters is worthy of death even by a sage; a man who betrays Shiva is worthy of death by all.
Thus deciding, the wise Veda, younger brother of Sindhu: "Whose is this sinful act, of some sinful wretch?
He who destroys the worship made with divine forest flowers, tubers, roots and fruits, and does another worship
with meat and tree leaves — he shall be killed by me." Thinking thus, the wise one, hiding his body then,
I shall see that sinner, the performer of worship to Ishvara. In the meantime the hunter came to the god as before,
worshipping him as usual; then Adikesha said:
O hunter of great mind, you are tired — again and again; "Why did you come so late? Without you, dear, I am distressed; I find no happiness; be comforted, son."
Hearing the god speak thus to him and seeing, Veda grew angry, filled with astonishment, and said nothing.
The hunter, having done the worship as usual, went to his house; Veda, enraged, came and said to the Lord:

This hunter is fond of sin, devoid of rites and knowledge, fond of killing creatures, cruel, merciless to all beings,
brahmapuran:169:28	of low birth, knowing nothing, without regard for teachers' succession, always acting improperly, who has not conquered the whole herd of cows (?).
brahmapuran:169:29	You showed yourself to him and will say nothing to me. I, Lord, of firm vows, perform worship with mantra procedure.
brahmapuran:169:30	Having you as sole refuge, always, without wife and son, this hunter makes worship to you with foul meat.
brahmapuran:169:31	That the Lord is pleased with him and not with me is a great wonder. I shall punish this injurious Bhilla.
brahmapuran:169:32	One may be angry yet pleased with the gentle, so too with the wicked; therefore I shall surely drop a rock on his head.
When Veda had said this, the Lord, laughing, said:
Wait until tomorrow; afterwards drop the rock on my head.
Saying "So be it," Veda too laid down the rock with his arm and, restraining that anger, said "I shall do it tomorrow."
Then in the morning, having come and done bathing and the rest, Veda, performing worship as usual, saw on the head
of the linga a wound and a terrible stream flowing with blood. Veda, astonished, thought, "What is this on the linga's head?
Whose great portent will it indicate?" With clay and cow-dung and kusha and Ganga water
he washed it and did the worship as usual. In the meantime the hunter came, free of sin,
and saw within, on the head of the linga of Shankara Adikesha, a wound and blood.
Seeing it he said, "What is this wonder?" and with sharp arrows pierced himself into a hundred and a thousand parts.
Seeing the injury of his lord, who of good mind could bear it? He reviled himself repeatedly: "This happened while I live!
What a misfortune has befallen, alas, through evil fate!" Seeing that act of his, Mahadeva, greatly astonished, said to Veda, best of Veda-knowers:

See, wise one, this hunter, a devotee full of feeling. You touched my head with clay, kusha and water.
brahmapuran:169:45	By this, Brahmin, my very self was suddenly given. Where there is devotion, love, power or consideration — therefore I shall give boons to him first, and afterwards to you, best of Brahmins.
The Lord Maheshvara offered the hunter a choice of boons. The hunter said to the Lord: "What remains as your offering,
let that be ours, lord; let a holy place be named by my name; let it give the fruit of all sacrifices by mere remembrance."
The Lord said "So be it"; then that excellent holy place, Bhilla-tirtha, became the cause of cutting off the whole mass of sin,
a bestower of great devotion to the feet of the revered Mahadeva, giving enjoyment and liberation by bathing, giving and the like. Shiva gave Veda also many kinds of boons.
Hearing that speech of the Brahmin who longed (for wealth), he agreed, took jewels quickly,
and handed his own wealth to Gautama. Wandering through countries comfortably with this wealth,
Having taken the wealth we shall return home. The merchant spoke truth, but that Brahmin was a deceiver;
the sinful-minded; and the merchant did not understand the sinful mind of the Brahmin. Taking leave of each other, without the knowledge of their parents,
the merchant and the Brahmin went from country to country for wealth. The Brahmin wished to steal the wealth in the merchant's hand:

By some means I must take that wealth. Ah, on earth there are thousands of lovely cities,
brahmapuran:170:20	women who, like goddesses of desire, give what is wished, charming ones here and there; what shall I do?
brahmapuran:170:21	If wealth is carefully gathered and given to women, they are enjoyed always, and then life is fruitful.
brahmapuran:170:22	Delighting always in dance and song, adorned by courtesans, how shall I enjoy that wealth that has come into my hand from the merchant?
Thus thinking, Gautama, smiling as it were, said to Manikundala: "Creatures, through unrighteousness alone,
obtain growth, happiness and desired things, no doubt. Righteous beings in the world are seen sharing sorrow.
So what use is dharma, which is the cause of sorrow as its only fruit?"
The merchant then said "No": "Happiness rests on dharma; in sin there is sorrow, fear, grief, poverty and pain. Where dharma is, there is liberation; does one's own dharma perish?"
While they argued thus, a wager arose between them: "Whoever's side proves stronger shall take the other's property."
Let us ask who is stronger, the righteous or the unrighteous; worldly reasoning is higher than the Veda; happiness comes from dharma in the world.
Arguing thus they asked all the people about the strength of dharma or adharma on earth.
Tell us as it is. They asked with vigour. Thus there some said, "Those who follow dharma
experience sorrow, and sinners are happy." In the wager he lost all his wealth and handed it to the Brahmin.
Manimat, best of the knowers of dharma, again praised dharma. The Brahmin said to Manimat: "Why do you praise dharma?" The merchant said "So," and the Brahmin again said:
I have won the wealth, merchant; why do you speak shamelessly? Dharma has been defeated by me, who act as I please.
Hearing that Brahmin's words, the merchant said, smiling:

Friend, I consider those in whom there is no dharma like chaff among grains and like insects among birds.
brahmapuran:170:36	Of the four human aims, dharma is called first; wealth and desire follow. That dharma stays in me; how do you say, best of Brahmins, that it has been defeated by me?
The Brahmin said again to the merchant: "Let the wager be (our) hands." The merchant agreed. Going back, they spoke again.
As before, going to the people, the Brahmin said, "I have won." Then, having cut off his hands, he said: "How do you now regard dharma?" Thus challenged by the Brahmin, the merchant said:
I hold dharma alone to be supreme, even with life-breath in my throat. Mother, father, friend, kinsman — dharma alone is such for embodied beings.
Arguing thus, the Brahmin became rich, and the merchant was robbed there of both arms and wealth.
Wandering thus they reached the Ganga and Hari, lord of yogis; by chance, best of sages, they spoke again to one another.
The merchant praised the Ganga, the lord of yogis, and dharma alone; in great anger the Brahmin again reviled the merchant:
Wealth gone, hands cut off, you remain only alive; if you speak otherwise, I shall cut off your head with a sword.
The merchant, laughing, said again to Gautama directly:

I hold dharma alone supreme; do as you wish. Brahmins, teachers, gods, the Vedas, dharma, Janardana —
brahmapuran:170:46	the sinner who reviles them is not to be touched; the evil-conducted, sinful, defiler of dharma is to be ignored.
Then he said in anger: "If you praise dharma, let our lives be the stake here, sage."
When Gautama said this, the merchant said "So be it." Again the two asked the people, and the people spoke.
In front of the lord of yogis, on the south bank of the Gautami, the Brahmin threw down the merchant, tore out his eyes and said:
You have come to this state, merchant, from constant praise of dharma: wealth gone, eyes gone, hands cut off. You are asked, friend; I go; do not say it again in conversation.
When he had gone, the merchant thought in his heart: "Alas, Hari, what misfortune has happened to me, who had my mind solely on dharma?"
That best of merchants Kundala, without wealth, without arms, without eyes, fell into grief, still remembering dharma only.
Thinking in many ways he lay on the ground, motionless, without enthusiasm, fallen into an ocean of sorrow.
At day's end, in the night, when the moon's disc had risen, on the eleventh of the bright half, Vibhishana came there.
Having duly worshipped the lord of yogis and bathed in the Gautami Ganga, with his son and surrounded by Rakshasas,
Vibhishana's son, like a second Vibhishana, famed as Vaibhishani, saw him and spoke.
Hearing the merchant's words, that knower of dharma reported it as it was to his father, the great-souled lord of Lanka; and the lord of Lanka said lovingly to his virtuous son:

The glorious Rama is my teacher, my honoured friend is Hanuman, famed; by him the great mountain was brought.
brahmapuran:170:59	Earlier, when a task arose, the mountain, refuge of all herbs, was taken by him and he came to the Himalaya.
brahmapuran:170:60	'Vishalyakarani' and 'Mritasanjivani': bringing them, the greatly wise one gave them to Rama, of unwearied action.
